node-1.label: Diffuse painful pustular lesions on face, trunk, hands, feet, ankles, and penis

node-2.label: Patient is a 33-year-old Hispanic bisexual man with HIV diagnosed 8 years prior and not receiving antiretroviral therapy; CD4 count 3 cells/mm³ (0%), viral load 43,751 copies/mL at presentation

node-3.label: Initial presentation included dysuria and penile discharge; two weeks later the patient was hospitalized due to worsening diffuse pustular lesions

why.why: Skin biopsy showing viral inclusions and positive DNA PCR with F13L gene mutations by whole genome sequencing confirm an orthopoxvirus (mpox) infection, making disseminated infection essentially confirmed. Negative HSV, VZV, and fungal tests exclude other common disseminated pathogens, and the patient's profound HIV immunosuppression (CD4 3 cells/mm³) with progression from genitourinary symptoms to diffuse pustular lesions strongly supports a disseminated infectious process.

The confirmed pathogen is orthopoxvirus (mpox), which is not a classic sexually transmitted infection, although it can be transmitted through close or sexual contact. Initial genitourinary symptoms and sexual history provide limited support, but negative HSV, VZV, and fungal tests rule out classic disseminated STIs, and positive mpox PCR redirects the diagnosis to disseminated mpox infection. Confidence is therefore reduced from 0.3 to 0.2.

Skin biopsy viral inclusions and positive DNA PCR with F13L gene mutations confirm an infectious orthopoxvirus etiology, directly refuting a noninfectious pustular dermatosis. The patient's untreated HIV immunosuppression and clinical progression further support an infectious process, so noninfectious pustular disease is essentially excluded.

node-8.label: DNA PCR with whole genome sequencing detects F13L gene mutations confirming orthopoxvirus (mpox)

node-9.label: HSV, VZV, and fungal tests are negative

why.why: Skin biopsy viral inclusions and DNA PCR with F13L mutations confirm mpox; profound HIV immunosuppression, diffuse pustules, and progression from genitourinary symptoms support dissemination. Negative HSV, VZV, and fungal tests exclude common mimics. The laboratory physician’s note of repeated skin PCR positivity adds further support for systemic infection. However, blood/CSF mpox PCR and visceral imaging remain unavailable, so direct hematogenous/organ dissemination is not confirmed. Therefore disseminated mpox remains the leading diagnosis with confidence 0.92.

node-11.label: Blood or CSF mpox PCR and species-level clade/blood dissemination results were not obtained, lacking direct hematogenous confirmation

why.why: As a refinement of disseminated infection, this is supported by confirmed mpox F13L mutations on skin PCR, viral inclusions, diffuse pustular lesions, and negative HSV/VZV/fungal tests. Repeated skin PCR positivity noted by the laboratory physician strengthens the case. Blood/CSF mpox PCR and visceral imaging remain unavailable, so direct systemic/organ dissemination is not confirmed, keeping confidence at 0.92.

attrs.why: HSV can cause disseminated pustular lesions in severely immunocompromised patients, and the initial genitourinary symptoms could suggest an STI. However, HSV testing is negative, and the confirmed orthopoxvirus etiology makes this much less likely. It remains a theoretical subcategory of disseminated infection but is largely excluded by available evidence.

VZV infection can produce vesiculopustular skin lesions and disseminate in immunosuppression. However, VZV testing is negative, and the skin biopsy findings are consistent with mpox rather than VZV. Therefore, although it is a possible refinement of disseminated infection, the evidence strongly argues against it.

Fungal infections, such as disseminated candidiasis or histoplasmosis, can occur in advanced HIV with CD4 count of 3 cells/mm³ and may involve skin. However, fungal tests are negative, and the skin biopsy showing viral inclusions plus positive mpox PCR points to a viral etiology, making disseminated fungal infection an unlikely refinement of the current frontier.

why.why: As a refinement of disseminated infection, this is supported by confirmed mpox F13L mutations on skin PCR, viral inclusions, diffuse pustular lesions, and negative HSV/VZV/fungal tests. Repeated skin PCR positivity noted by the laboratory physician strengthens the case. Blood/CSF mpox PCR and visceral imaging remain unavailable, so direct systemic/organ dissemination is not confirmed, keeping confidence at 0.92.

attrs.why: HSV can cause disseminated pustular lesions in severely immunocompromised patients, and the initial genitourinary symptoms could suggest an STI. However, HSV testing is negative, and the confirmed orthopoxvirus etiology makes this much less likely. It remains a theoretical subcategory of disseminated infection but is largely excluded by available evidence.

VZV infection can produce vesiculopustular skin lesions and disseminate in immunosuppression. However, VZV testing is negative, and the skin biopsy findings are consistent with mpox rather than VZV. Therefore, although it is a possible refinement of disseminated infection, the evidence strongly argues against it.

Fungal infections, such as disseminated candidiasis or histoplasmosis, can occur in advanced HIV with CD4 count of 3 cells/mm³ and may involve skin. However, fungal tests are negative, and the skin biopsy showing viral inclusions plus positive mpox PCR points to a viral etiology, making disseminated fungal infection an unlikely refinement of the current frontier.
